Ciechanowiec New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Ciechanowiec, Poland

Not demolished. Ciechanowiec, first documented in the 13th century and a notable Arian movement center in the 16th, recorded its first Jews in 1523, forming an independent kehilla likely by the second half of the 17th century - eventually the fourth-largest kehilla in the Podlasie region, making up 60% of the population by the 18th century's second half. After 1807's Treaty of Tilsit split the town between Russian and Polish rule, each side developed its own sizeable Jewish community (about 900 on the Polish side, 2,500 on the Russian side) with separate synagogue boards. Germans established a ghetto in October 1941; a year later, shortly before liquidation, about 285 Jews were massacred near Pobirki, with survivors deported to Treblinka II and Majdanek. This 'new' cemetery, likely established around 1850, was later used as an illegal sand mine; recovered tombstones were stored for years at the local Krzysztof Kluk Agricultural Museum before a 2008 restoration marked the boundaries with boulders and returned about 30 tombstones (dated 1853-1934).
